Applying session controls with Conditional Access app control
questions.explanation: Cloud Discovery and session controls are core CASB capabilities. Patching domain controllers and disk encryption are not.

questions.question: An auditor asks for Microsoft's ISO 27001 certificate and SOC reports for Azure. Where can you find these?

questions.question: Which Microsoft privacy principle states that customer email, chat and files are not used for advertising targeting?
options: Benefits to you from data collected
Control over how data is used
questions.explanation: No content-based targeting means Microsoft does not use what is in your content to target ads. Control and transparency concern choices and clarity, and benefits to you concern value in return for data.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of Microsoft's six privacy principles?

questions.question: The Service Trust Portal provides audit reports and compliance documentation about Microsoft cloud services.
questions.explanation: It is the central location for audit reports, certifications, compliance guides and whitepapers.

questions.question: An organization wants templates and step-by-step improvement actions to help it comply with GDPR. Which tool should it use?

The amount of data stored in SharePoint sites
Whether the organization is legally compliant

questions.question: In Compliance Manager, who can perform improvement actions?
options: Microsoft for some actions and the customer for others
Only Microsoft can perform any of the actions
Only the customer can perform any of the actions
Only external auditors can perform the actions
questions.explanation: Some improvement actions are managed by Microsoft and others by the customer; both contribute to the score.

questions.question: A high compliance score guarantees that an organization meets all legal obligations.
questions.explanation: The score is a guide to progress on improvement actions. It does not constitute a guarantee or certification of compliance.

questions.question: Which two items are part of Compliance Manager? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Assessments and improvement actions are core. Safe Attachments belongs to Defender for Office 365 and Cloud Discovery to Defender for Cloud Apps.

questions.question: A compliance team wants to find documents that contain credit card numbers anywhere in the organization. Which Purview capability identifies them?
options: Safe Links in Defender for Office 365
Access reviews in Entra ID Governance
questions.explanation: Sensitive information types detect patterns such as credit card numbers. The others belong to other solutions.

questions.explanation: Content explorer gives a current view of classified items. Activity explorer shows what happened to them over time.

questions.question: Which tool shows a history of actions on labeled content, such as when a label was changed or a file was copied?
questions.explanation: Activity explorer provides a timeline of labeling and handling activities.

questions.question: Which feature adds encryption and a "Confidential" watermark that stays with a document when it is emailed outside the company?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity labels can encrypt and mark content, and the protection follows the file.

questions.question: Administrators created a sensitivity label, but users do not see it in Word. What is most likely missing?
options: A sensitivity label policy publishing the label to the users
A data loss prevention policy for email
An access review of group members
questions.explanation: Labels become available to users only after they are published through a label policy.

questions.question: A policy must block users from emailing documents that contain social security numbers to outside recipients, showing a policy tip first. Which solution fits?
questions.explanation: DLP detects sensitive content and enforces actions such as policy tips and blocking sharing.

questions.question: Which feature prevents sensitive files from being copied to a USB drive on company laptops?
questions.explanation: Endpoint DLP monitors and restricts actions on sensitive files on Windows and macOS devices.

questions.question: A law requires all Exchange mailboxes to be kept for seven years and then deleted. What is the simplest approach?
options: A retention policy applied to Exchange mailboxes
A sensitivity label applied to each individual email
Manually tagging every email with a retention label
Enabling security defaults in Entra ID

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes a retention label from a retention policy?
options: A label is applied to individual items and can declare a record; a policy applies to whole locations
A label applies to whole locations; a policy is applied to single items and records
They are identical and the terms can be used interchangeably
A label only encrypts files and has no retention settings

questions.question: An organization needs documents that cannot be edited or deleted for the duration of their retention period, with proof of disposal at the end. Which capability fits?

questions.question: A sensitivity label can apply encryption that stays with the file.
questions.explanation: Label protection settings include encryption and access control that persist with the content.

questions.question: Retention policies must be applied by each user to every individual document.
questions.explanation: Retention policies are applied by administrators to locations, so users do not tag documents themselves. Item-level labels are the option users can apply.

questions.question: Which two actions can a DLP policy take when it detects sensitive content? (Choose two.)

Join the device to the domain

questions.question: Which two are used by Purview to classify data? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: SITs and trainable classifiers identify content. NSGs and Safe Links belong to network and email security.

questions.question: A company wants to detect employees who copy large amounts of files to personal cloud storage shortly before they resign. Which solution fits?
questions.explanation: Insider risk management uses indicators and policy templates such as data theft by departing users to raise alerts.

questions.question: How does insider risk management help protect user privacy?
options: Usernames are pseudonymized by default and access is role-based
It never records any user activity at all
It publishes every alert to all employees for transparency
It disables auditing for the monitored users
questions.explanation: Privacy is built in through pseudonymization and role-based access to alerts and cases.

questions.question: Legal counsel needs to preserve and collect mailbox and file content for a lawsuit, placing a hold on it. Which Purview solution is used?
questions.explanation: eDiscovery lets you create cases, place legal holds, search, review and export content.

questions.question: Which eDiscovery edition adds custodian management, review sets and near-duplicate detection?
questions.explanation: Premium extends Standard with custodians, review sets and advanced analytics for complex cases.

questions.question: An investigator needs to find who deleted a file in SharePoint last month. Which solution provides this?
questions.explanation: Audit records user and admin activities so you can search for who did what and when.

questions.question: Which feature distinguishes Audit (Premium) from Audit (Standard)?
options: Audit log retention policies and longer retention
Being able to search audit logs at all
Being turned on by default for the tenant
Exporting audit records to a CSV file

questions.question: What is the default audit log retention for Audit (Standard)?

questions.question: Insider risk management is designed mainly to stop external attackers who have no access to the organization.
questions.explanation: It focuses on risky activity by people who already have legitimate access, such as employees and contractors.

questions.question: eDiscovery can place a legal hold so that content is preserved while a case is investigated.
questions.explanation: Holds preserve content, even if users try to delete it, while the matter is open.

questions.question: Which two are Audit (Premium) capabilities? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Premium adds retention policies and high-value events. The other options are not audit features.

lessons.title: Security and Compliance Concepts
lessons.summary: Shared responsibility, defense in depth, Zero Trust, encryption, hashing and GRC.
lessons.reading:
Security starts with who is responsible for what. Under the shared responsibility model, Microsoft always secures the physical datacenter, network and hosts, and the customer always secures its own information and data, its devices, and its accounts and identities. The operating system, network controls and applications move between the two as you go from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS, so on a virtual machine you patch the OS and on a platform service Microsoft does.

Two ideas describe how to build protection. Defense in depth stacks independent layers, from physical security and identity through the perimeter, network, compute and application to data, so a single failure does not expose everything. Zero Trust changes the assumption underneath: it treats the network as hostile, so every request is checked. Its three principles are verify explicitly, use least privilege access, and assume breach.

Cryptography supports these goals. Encryption makes data unreadable without a key, either symmetrically (one shared key, fast, used for bulk data) or asymmetrically (a public and private key pair, used for key exchange and signatures). Encryption protects data at rest and in transit. Hashing is different: it is a one-way fingerprint used to check integrity and to store passwords safely.

Compliance and risk sit around the technology. Governance, risk and compliance (GRC) is the shared discipline of setting rules and accountability, identifying and reducing risk, and proving that laws and standards are met. Data residency is where data is stored, and data sovereignty is the legal reality that the laws of that location apply to it.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to security? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals:
Think of renting an apartment in a managed building. The landlord guards the front door and the building structure (the provider's side), but you still lock your own door, protect your keys and decide who you let in (your side). That split is shared responsibility.

Defense in depth is a bank with a street door, a guard, a vault and a safe-deposit box. Zero Trust is a bank that checks ID every time you walk in, even if the teller knows your face.
commonTraps: Data, devices and identities are the customer's in every service model, even SaaS.
Hashing is one-way and encryption is reversible with a key; do not mix them up.
Zero Trust is a mindset of verifying every request, not a single product or a stronger firewall.
lessons.scenario: A company moves a HR app from its own server room to Azure. The cloud provider now handles the building, power and hardware, but the company still decides who can sign in, still protects employee data, and still has to patch the VM operating system if it chose IaaS. Moving to a PaaS database would hand the OS patching to Microsoft, but not the question of who may read the records.
lessons.onTheJob: In practice the shared responsibility model is the first slide in any cloud risk review. Auditors ask "which layer is yours?" and gaps appear where a team assumes the provider covers identity or data classification. Writing the split down per workload, and mapping each customer-side item to an owner, prevents most of the arguments after an incident.

lessons.title: Identity Concepts
lessons.summary: Identity as the perimeter, authentication, authorization, identity providers, directories and federation.
lessons.reading:
When data and apps live in the cloud and people work from anywhere, the corporate network is no longer the edge that defines what is protected. The identity requesting access is, so identity is described as the primary security perimeter. Attackers know this and go after credentials, which is why strong verification matters more than ever.

Two words must stay separate. Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. Authentication happens first. An identity provider (IdP) creates and manages identities and performs authentication for applications, handing them a signed token instead of a password. Microsoft Entra ID is an identity provider.

A directory service stores identity information centrally. Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is Microsoft's on-premises directory, based on domain controllers and protocols such as Kerberos, NTLM and LDAP. Microsoft Entra ID is a different, cloud-native service built for web protocols. Many organizations run both and connect them with hybrid identity.

Federation is a trust between identity providers, so a user authenticated by one organization can reach another's apps with single sign-on. SAML, WS-Federation and OpenID Connect are typical protocols, and OAuth 2.0 handles delegated authorization.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to identity? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals:
Showing your passport at airport check-in is authentication: it proves who you are. The boarding pass then says which flight you may board, which is authorization.

Federation is like two countries agreeing to honor each other's visas. The traveler is checked once by their home country, and the other country trusts that check.
commonTraps: Authentication proves identity; authorization grants permissions. The first does not imply the second.
Entra ID is not AD DS in the cloud; they use different protocols and are often combined.
OAuth 2.0 is about authorization. OpenID Connect adds authentication on top.
lessons.scenario: Fabrikam employees open a supplier's portal by clicking "Sign in with your work account". Fabrikam's Entra ID authenticates them and sends a signed token; the supplier's app trusts it and only then checks which orders the employee may see. The first step is authentication through federation, the second is authorization.
lessons.onTheJob: Most breaches in the cloud begin with a stolen or phished credential rather than a broken firewall, so identity teams spend their time on strong sign-in and clean permissions. When a team says "the app handles its own logins", ask who owns the password store: moving to a shared identity provider removes a whole class of risk and gives one place to enforce MFA.

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra ID and Identity Types
lessons.summary: What Entra ID is, the editions, the identity types, workload identities and hybrid identity.
lessons.reading:
Microsoft Entra ID, formerly Azure Active Directory, is Microsoft's cloud identity and access management service. Each organization has its own dedicated instance, called a tenant, which holds its users, groups, devices and applications. Entra ID signs people in to Microsoft 365, the Azure portal and thousands of SaaS apps, and it comes in Free, P1 and P2 tiers, with ID Governance as an add-on. The Entra family also includes External ID, Verified ID, Workload ID, Domain Services and the Global Secure Access services.

Entra ID manages several types of identity. People are users, and external partners can be invited as guests (B2B collaboration). Devices have identities too, as registered, joined or hybrid joined devices. Software gets workload identities: app registrations, service principals and managed identities, so code never has to run as a person. A managed identity is created and rotated by Azure, which removes secrets from code.

Hybrid identity connects on-premises Active Directory with Entra ID so users have one identity. Microsoft Entra Connect Sync or Cloud Sync copies accounts to the cloud, and passwords can be validated through password hash synchronization, pass-through authentication or federation. Microsoft Entra Domain Services is a separate managed service for legacy apps that need domain join, LDAP or Kerberos in Azure.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to Entra ID? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A tenant is like a company's badge office. It issues badges to employees (users), guests and contractors (guest users), laptops (devices), and even to the building's robots (workload identities). Hybrid identity is the badge office keeping its on-site records and its online records in sync.
commonTraps: Guests sign in with their own home credentials; you do not create passwords for them.
A workload identity represents software, not a person.
Entra Domain Services is a managed AD DS-like service, not the same as Entra ID.
lessons.scenario: A retailer keeps its staff accounts in on-premises Active Directory but wants everyone on Microsoft 365. It installs Entra Connect to synchronize accounts, so each person has one identity. A web app in Azure reads secrets from Key Vault through a managed identity, and a vendor's consultant is invited as a B2B guest with her own company login.
lessons.onTheJob: The most common surprise is licensing: a feature in a demo turns out to need P1 or P2, so check the tier before promising it. Also watch for service accounts with passwords in config files; swapping them for managed identities is one of the cheapest security wins in an Azure estate.

lessons.title: Authentication in Microsoft Entra
lessons.summary: MFA, passwordless sign-in, passkeys, security defaults, SSPR and password protection.
lessons.reading:
Passwords alone are the weakest link, so Entra ID supports several stronger ways to prove identity. Multifactor authentication combines at least two kinds of proof: something you know, something you have, and something you are. The method matters too: the Microsoft Authenticator app and passkeys are preferred, while SMS and voice calls are supported but weaker because they can be intercepted or socially engineered.

Passwordless sign-in goes further and removes the password. Windows Hello for Business, Microsoft Authenticator and passkeys or FIDO2 security keys all use a private key held on the device, unlocked by a PIN or biometric. Passkeys are phishing-resistant because the credential only works for the real site, so a fake login page captures nothing reusable.

For organizations without Conditional Access, security defaults offer a free baseline that requires MFA registration, protects administrators and blocks legacy authentication. Self-service password reset lets people recover their own accounts, and password writeback returns the new password to on-premises AD DS. Entra Password Protection blocks weak passwords with a global banned list, adds a custom list with P1, and smart lockout slows guessing attacks.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to MFA? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals:
Withdrawing cash needs your card (something you have) and your PIN (something you know). One without the other is useless. MFA applies the same idea to sign-in.

A passkey is like a key that only fits the one lock it was made for and refuses to open a lookalike door built by a thief.
commonTraps: MFA needs different factor categories; two passwords are still one factor type.
SMS and voice work for MFA but are not phishing-resistant.
Security defaults and Conditional Access are not used together.
lessons.scenario: A 30-person firm with only basic licenses turns on security defaults, and everyone has to register the Authenticator app. Later the firm buys P1, turns security defaults off and moves to Conditional Access, adds a custom banned list with its company name, and enables self-service password reset.
lessons.onTheJob: Rolling out MFA is mostly a people problem. Registration campaigns, a clear help desk script for lost phones, and a Temporary Access Pass for new starters matter as much as the technology. Expect pushback on SMS removal; show the phishing numbers.

lessons.title: Access Management, Protection and Governance
lessons.summary: Conditional Access, Entra roles vs. Azure RBAC, ID Governance, access reviews, PIM and ID Protection.
lessons.reading:
Conditional Access is the policy engine of Zero Trust. It evaluates signals such as the user, location, device, application and risk after the first sign-in, then decides to block, or to grant access with requirements such as MFA or a compliant device. Report-only mode lets administrators see a policy's effect before enforcing it. Conditional Access needs P1, and risk signals need P2.

Entra roles and Azure RBAC are two different permission systems. Entra roles, such as Global Administrator or User Administrator, control the directory. Azure RBAC roles, such as Owner, Contributor and Reader, control Azure resources and apply at management group, subscription, resource group or resource scope. Give the least privileged role that does the job, and keep Global Administrators few. Global Secure Access, with Entra Internet Access and Entra Private Access, is Microsoft's SSE solution for identity-aware access to the internet and private apps.

Identity governance keeps access appropriate over time. Entitlement management bundles resources into access packages, lifecycle workflows automate joiners, movers and leavers, and access reviews have owners or managers recertify access, removing it automatically if it is no longer needed. Privileged Identity Management turns standing admin rights into eligible ones that must be activated just in time, with approval, justification and MFA. Entra ID Protection scores sign-in risk and user risk from detections such as leaked credentials and impossible travel, and drives automated responses through Conditional Access.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to access control? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Conditional Access is a bouncer with a checklist: "Are you on the list? Is it your usual door? Is your ID valid? Then come in, but show me a second ID if you came in through the back." PIM is a key cabinet: admin keys are signed out for an hour with a reason, not carried around all year. Access reviews are the quarterly check that everyone with a key still needs one.
commonTraps: Entra roles manage the directory; Azure RBAC manages Azure resources. Owning one does not grant the other.
Conditional Access needs P1, but risk-based conditions need P2 because they use ID Protection.
PIM makes admins eligible, not permanent; they must activate the role.
lessons.scenario: Contoso wants finance staff to use MFA from outside the office and wants high-risk sign-ins blocked. It creates a Conditional Access policy in report-only mode, checks the logs, then enforces it. Administrators become eligible in PIM and activate roles for two hours with a justification, and a quarterly access review asks managers to confirm which guests still need Teams.
lessons.onTheJob: Conditional Access policies that lock out everyone, including the admin who created them, are a classic incident. Keep emergency access accounts excluded and monitored, and always begin in report-only mode. Reviews and PIM only pay off when someone actually reads the results, so assign owners.

lessons.title: Core Infrastructure Security in Azure
lessons.summary: DDoS Protection, Azure Firewall, WAF, network security groups, segmentation, Bastion and Key Vault.
lessons.reading:
Azure offers a toolbox of network and platform controls that map to different threats. Azure DDoS Protection guards availability: every public IP gets free infrastructure protection, and the paid IP Protection and Network Protection tiers add adaptive tuning and attack analytics, with Network Protection also providing Rapid Response support and cost protection.

For traffic control, network security groups (NSGs) are the basic filter: allow and deny rules on source, destination, port and protocol, attached to subnets or network interfaces and processed from the lowest priority number up. Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful firewall for a whole virtual network with network and application rules, FQDN filtering and threat intelligence, and its Premium SKU adds TLS inspection and an intrusion detection and prevention system. Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) sits in front of web apps on Application Gateway or Front Door and blocks web exploits such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Segmenting a network into virtual networks and subnets limits how far an attacker can move.

Two services reduce exposure of access and secrets. Azure Bastion gives RDP and SSH to VMs straight from the portal over TLS, so the VMs need no public IPs. Azure Key Vault stores secrets, keys and certificates, controls access with Entra ID, and supports hardware security modules.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to network security? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture an office park. DDoS Protection is the road barrier that keeps a mob from blocking the entrance. The firewall is the main gate guard checking everyone in and out, the WAF is the receptionist who recognizes a conman at the front desk, and NSGs are the key-card readers on each floor. Bastion is the secure visitor lift, and Key Vault is the locked safe where the master keys are kept.
commonTraps: NSGs work on IPs, ports and protocols (layers 3 and 4); they cannot see SQL injection. That is WAF.
TLS inspection and IDPS are Azure Firewall Premium only.
Cost protection and Rapid Response belong to DDoS Network Protection, not IP Protection.
lessons.scenario: A company hosts a customer portal in Azure. A WAF in front of Application Gateway blocks injection attempts, DDoS Network Protection covers the public IPs, NSGs separate the web and database subnets, administrators reach VMs through Bastion with no public IPs, and the app reads its database password from Key Vault using a managed identity.
lessons.onTheJob: Teams often deploy a firewall and a WAF and think one covers both jobs. Treat them as separate layers, and check NSG rule order whenever traffic is unexpectedly blocked: one broad deny with a low number silently overrides everything after it.

lessons.title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud
lessons.summary: CSPM, secure score, recommendations, standards and cloud workload protection.
lessons.reading:
Microsoft Defender for Cloud is a cloud-native application protection platform that covers Azure, AWS, Google Cloud and on-premises resources. It has two halves. Cloud security posture management (CSPM) finds misconfigurations and weaknesses and tells you how to fix them. Cloud workload protection adds threat detection and advanced protection for running workloads.

Foundational CSPM is free: it provides an asset inventory, security recommendations based on the Microsoft cloud security benchmark, and a secure score that rises as recommendations are remediated. The paid Defender CSPM plan adds attack path analysis, the cloud security explorer, agentless scanning, governance rules and regulatory compliance reporting. Security policies and standards turn a requirement such as NIST or ISO 27001 into checks, so each failing check becomes a recommendation.

Workload protection is enabled per resource type through Defender plans, such as Defender for Servers, Containers, Storage, Databases, App Service and Key Vault. Defender for Servers also offers just-in-time VM access, which closes management ports until an approved request opens them briefly.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to posture management? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: CSPM is a building inspector who walks the property with a checklist and hands you a punch list of unlocked doors. Workload protection is the security guard on duty who watches for break-ins while the building is in use.
commonTraps: Defender for Cloud is not Defender for Cloud Apps. One protects infrastructure, the other is a CASB for SaaS.
Secure score, recommendations and asset inventory are free; attack path analysis is paid.
A higher secure score means lower risk, not more alerts.
lessons.scenario: A company runs workloads in Azure and AWS. It connects both to Defender for Cloud, works down recommendations that raise the secure score the most, enables Defender CSPM to see attack paths to its customer database, and turns on Defender for Servers so that RDP is closed unless an engineer requests access.
lessons.onTheJob: Recommendation lists can run to hundreds of items. Sort by impact on secure score and by attack paths, assign each to a resource owner, and expect some to be accepted risk rather than fixed. Costs for Defender plans scale with resources, so enable them deliberately.

lessons.title: Microsoft Sentinel
lessons.summary: SIEM and SOAR concepts, data connectors, analytics rules, hunting, workbooks and playbooks.
lessons.reading:
A security information and event management (SIEM) system collects logs and events from across an environment, correlates them to spot threats, and keeps the evidence for investigation. A security orchestration, automation and response (SOAR) system adds automatic reaction, such as disabling an account or isolating a device, so analysts are not handling every alert by hand.

Microsoft Sentinel is Microsoft's cloud-native SIEM and SOAR. Data connectors feed it from Microsoft services, other clouds and third-party tools. Analytics rules query that data and raise alerts, and related alerts are grouped into incidents for investigation. User and entity behavior analytics flags activity that departs from a baseline, and imported threat intelligence matches known bad indicators. Analysts can hunt proactively with Kusto Query Language and bookmark what they find, and workbooks provide dashboards.

Response is automated with playbooks, which are Azure Logic Apps workflows, and automation rules that decide when to assign, tag, close or trigger them. Microsoft is moving Sentinel into the Microsoft Defender portal, and has said Azure portal support ends after March 31, 2027.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to SIEM? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Sentinel is the security operations room of a large building: cameras and door logs from every floor stream into one wall of screens (SIEM), the system flags suspicious patterns, and standard procedures such as locking doors or paging a guard run automatically (SOAR).
commonTraps: Sentinel is both SIEM and SOAR, not just one of them.
Playbooks respond, workbooks visualize, connectors ingest, rules detect.
Sentinel collects from any source; Defender XDR focuses on correlating Microsoft workloads.
lessons.scenario: A bank connects Entra ID, Microsoft 365, firewall and Azure logs to Sentinel. An analytics rule detects impossible travel, creates an incident, and an automation rule runs a playbook that disables the account and messages the SOC. Analysts later hunt with KQL for similar patterns.
lessons.onTheJob: Sentinel bills by data ingested, so the real work is choosing what to connect and keeping noisy sources under control. A rule nobody tunes becomes alert fatigue; assign an owner to each detection and retire the ones that never produce a real finding.

lessons.title: Threat Protection with Microsoft Defender XDR
lessons.summary: XDR, the Defender portal, and Defender for Office 365, Endpoint, Cloud Apps, Identity, Vulnerability Management and Threat Intelligence.
lessons.reading:
Extended detection and response (XDR) correlates signals from many domains into one picture. Microsoft Defender XDR does this for Microsoft workloads and brings several products together: Defender for Office 365 protects email and collaboration, Defender for Endpoint protects devices, Defender for Identity watches on-premises Active Directory, and Defender for Cloud Apps acts as a cloud access security broker. Alerts from all of them are merged into incidents, and automated investigation and response and automatic attack disruption help contain threats quickly.

Defender for Office 365 uses Safe Attachments (sandbox detonation) and Safe Links (time-of-click URL checks), with Plan 2 adding Threat Explorer, automated investigation and attack simulation training. Defender for Endpoint offers attack surface reduction, next-generation antivirus and endpoint detection and response on Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS and Android. Defender for Identity uses sensors on domain controllers to spot reconnaissance, lateral movement and pass-the-hash. Defender for Cloud Apps discovers shadow IT, assesses app risk, connects to SaaS apps and applies session controls.

Defender Vulnerability Management continuously finds and prioritizes software weaknesses. Microsoft Threat Intelligence and its threat analytics reports tell you which emerging threats matter to your estate. All of this is managed in the Microsoft Defender portal, which shows the features your licenses include.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to XDR? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Instead of separate alarms for the mailroom, the doors, the staff directory and the vendors, XDR puts every alarm on one board and notices when the suspicious mailroom delivery, the odd badge swipe and the unknown vendor visit are all one break-in attempt.
commonTraps: Defender for Cloud (infrastructure) and Defender for Cloud Apps (SaaS CASB) are different products.
Defender for Identity covers on-premises AD; Entra ID Protection covers cloud identity risk.
Phishing simulation and Threat Explorer are Defender for Office 365 Plan 2.
lessons.scenario: A user clicks a phishing link. Safe Links blocks the page at click time, but one device is infected via another route. Defender for Endpoint detects the malware, Defender for Identity sees a lateral-movement attempt against a domain controller, and Defender XDR joins the alerts into one incident that the team investigates in the Defender portal.
lessons.onTheJob: The portal consolidation matters in practice: analysts stop swivelling between consoles, and automated investigation removes a lot of routine triage. Check license coverage early, because a missing product silently leaves a blind spot in the incident story.

lessons.title: Service Trust Portal, Privacy and Compliance Manager
lessons.summary: Where to find Microsoft's audit evidence, the privacy principles, the Purview portal and compliance score.
lessons.reading:
Compliance starts with trust. The Service Trust Portal is Microsoft's library of compliance evidence: audit reports, certifications such as ISO and SOC, compliance guides, penetration test results and whitepapers. Customers use it to show their own auditors how Microsoft meets standards.

Microsoft states six privacy principles: control, transparency, security, strong legal protections, no content-based targeting and benefits to you. Microsoft Priva is the privacy management product that helps find personal data and handle subject rights requests.

Day to day, administrators work in the Microsoft Purview portal, which hosts the data security, governance and compliance solutions. Compliance Manager is the tool to assess, track and improve compliance with regulations such as GDPR, ISO 27001 and HIPAA. An assessment holds controls, each with improvement actions that either Microsoft or you must carry out. Completing them raises the compliance score, a measure of progress that helps prioritize work. It is a guide, not a certificate: a high score does not prove legal compliance.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to compliance? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Compliance Manager is like a fitness tracker for regulations: it sets the targets (assessments), lists the exercises (improvement actions) and gives a score for how far along you are. The Service Trust Portal is the landlord's inspection certificates you show a bank.
commonTraps: Compliance score measures progress on improvement actions; it does not prove compliance.
The Service Trust Portal is for Microsoft's documents, not for classifying your own data.
Some improvement actions are managed by Microsoft and still count toward the score.
lessons.scenario: A healthcare provider preparing for an audit downloads Microsoft's ISO 27001 and SOC reports from the Service Trust Portal, then uses Compliance Manager's HIPAA assessment. It assigns improvement actions to teams and watches its compliance score rise as each action is completed.
lessons.onTheJob: Auditors want evidence, not scores. Keep screenshots and documents attached to each improvement action, and use the Service Trust Portal to answer "what does Microsoft do?" so your team only has to evidence its own part.

lessons.title: Information Protection and Data Lifecycle Management
lessons.summary: Classification, content and activity explorer, sensitivity labels, DLP, retention and records management.
lessons.reading:
Protecting data begins with knowing what you have. Data classification finds and tags content using sensitive information types (patterns such as credit card numbers), exact data match and trainable classifiers that learn what a category of document looks like. Content explorer then shows where classified or labeled items currently are, and activity explorer shows the history of what happened to them.

Sensitivity labels turn a classification into protection: a label can encrypt a file, add headers and watermarks, and restrict access, and it travels with the content. Labels reach users only after a sensitivity label policy publishes them, and the policy can set a default label, require labeling and demand justification to lower one. Data loss prevention (DLP) policies detect sensitive content and stop risky sharing with policy tips, blocks and alerts across Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams and, with Endpoint DLP, devices.

Data lifecycle management decides how long to keep content. A retention policy applies broadly to a location, such as every mailbox, and retains, deletes or both. A retention label applies to individual items, is published or auto-applied through a label policy, and can mark an item as a record. Records management uses a file plan and retention labels so records cannot be edited or deleted, with disposition review and proof of disposal.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to information protection? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A sensitivity label is a "Confidential" stamp and a lockbox for a document. DLP is the guard at the door who stops confidential papers leaving the building. A retention policy is the office rule that says all invoices are shredded after seven years, and a retention label is a sticky note on one contract saying keep this forever.
commonTraps: Content explorer shows what exists now; activity explorer shows what happened over time.
A label is not visible to users until a label policy publishes it.
Retention policy = whole location. Retention label = individual item (and can declare a record).
lessons.scenario: A law firm creates a "Client Confidential" sensitivity label that encrypts documents, and publishes it with a policy that makes labeling mandatory. A DLP policy blocks emailing labeled files outside the firm, a retention policy keeps all mailboxes for seven years, and a retention label declares signed contracts as records.
lessons.onTheJob: Start simple. Teams that launch ten labels with complex encryption see users give up or mislabel everything. Run in test mode, check activity explorer to see what really happens, then tighten DLP. Make sure legal agrees retention periods before you turn deletion on.

lessons.title: Insider Risk, eDiscovery and Audit
lessons.summary: Insider risk management, eDiscovery Standard and Premium, and Purview Audit.
lessons.reading:
Insider risk management looks for risky activity by people who already have access, such as copying files before resigning or sending sensitive data to personal email. Policy templates and indicators produce alerts that become cases, with privacy protections such as pseudonymized usernames and role-based access. Communication compliance is a separate solution that reviews messages for policy violations.

eDiscovery supports legal and regulatory investigations: create a case, place a legal hold so relevant content cannot be deleted, search, review and export. Standard covers cases, searches, holds and export, while Premium adds custodian management, review sets and advanced analytics for large or complex matters.

Purview Audit records who did what and when. Audit (Standard) is on by default and keeps records for 180 days. Audit (Premium) adds retention policies and longer retention, one year by default for Entra ID, Exchange, OneDrive and SharePoint records of properly licensed users and up to 10 years with an add-on, along with intelligent insights such as MailItemsAccessed and higher bandwidth to the Management Activity API.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to insider risk and eDiscovery? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Audit is the building's security-camera archive. Insider risk management is the analyst who notices a staff member carrying out boxes of files after handing in their notice. eDiscovery is the court-ordered process of freezing, collecting and handing over the relevant evidence.
commonTraps: Insider risk is about trusted people, not outside attackers.
Standard audit retention is 180 days; one-year-plus retention is Premium.
Insider risk management and communication compliance are separate solutions.
lessons.scenario: A manufacturer notices an engineer who handed in notice has been copying design files to a personal cloud account. Insider risk management raises an alert and a case. Months later a lawsuit begins: legal counsel opens an eDiscovery case, places holds on the engineer's mailbox and OneDrive, and the audit log confirms exactly what was accessed.
lessons.onTheJob: Involve HR and legal before turning insider risk on, because the signals are about people. Check licensing for the retention you promise to auditors: a one-year Premium default applies only to users with the right license.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: Microsoft Fundamentals exams give about 45 minutes and typically 40 to 60 questions. Pace yourself at under a minute per question and flag any you are unsure about.
Microsoft scores this 0 to 1000 with 700 to pass, not a flat percentage. Treat 75%+ in practice as a safe buffer, not an exact predictor.
The exam is breadth over depth: know what each product is for and which one fits a scenario, not how to configure it.

Most traps are look-alike product names (Defender for Cloud vs Defender for Cloud Apps, sensitivity labels vs retention labels, Entra roles vs Azure RBAC). Read the scenario for the one clue that separates them.

cheatSheet.heading: Concepts in one breath
points: Shared responsibility: customer always owns data, devices and identities; provider always owns the physical layer; the OS shifts with IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
Defense in depth = layers (physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application, data). Zero Trust = verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach.
Encryption is reversible with a key (symmetric = one key, asymmetric = key pair). Hashing is one-way and proves integrity.
Authentication = who you are. Authorization = what you may do. Federation = trust between identity providers.

cheatSheet.heading: Entra: licenses and identities
points: Free: users, groups, SSO, basic MFA and security defaults. P1: Conditional Access, dynamic groups, Application Proxy, password writeback. P2: ID Protection, PIM. ID Governance: entitlement management, access reviews, lifecycle workflows.

Identity types: users, groups, devices (registered, joined, hybrid joined) and workload identities (app registrations, service principals, managed identities). Guests use B2B collaboration with their own credentials.
Hybrid identity uses Entra Connect or Cloud Sync, with password hash synchronization, pass-through authentication or federation.

cheatSheet.heading: Entra: sign-in and access
points: MFA = two different factor categories. Passwordless = Windows Hello for Business, Authenticator, passkeys and FIDO2 keys. SMS and voice are the weakest.
Conditional Access = signals in, decision out (block or grant with controls). Use report-only mode first. Risk-based policies need P2.
Entra roles manage the directory; Azure RBAC manages Azure resources. PIM = eligible, time-limited, just-in-time. Access reviews = recertify.
Entra Private Access replaces VPN-style access to private apps. Entra Internet Access secures internet and SaaS traffic.

cheatSheet.heading: Azure infrastructure security: pick the tool
points: DDoS Protection = availability attacks. Network Protection adds Rapid Response, cost protection and a WAF discount; IP Protection is per IP.

NSG = free allow/deny by IP, port and protocol on subnets or NICs; lowest priority number wins. Azure Firewall = managed central firewall, FQDN rules and threat intelligence; Premium adds TLS inspection and IDPS.
WAF = web exploits (SQL injection, cross-site scripting) on Application Gateway, Front Door or CDN. Bastion = RDP/SSH over TLS with no public IP on the VM. Key Vault = secrets, keys and certificates.
Segment networks with VNets and subnets to limit lateral movement (assume breach).

cheatSheet.heading: Defender for Cloud and Sentinel
points: Defender for Cloud = CSPM (posture: secure score, recommendations, standards) plus cloud workload protection (Defender plans). Multicloud: Azure, AWS, Google Cloud.

Free Foundational CSPM: secure score, recommendations, asset inventory, Microsoft cloud security benchmark. Paid Defender CSPM: attack path analysis, cloud security explorer, agentless scanning, governance.

SIEM = collect, correlate, alert. SOAR = automate the response. Sentinel is both: connectors in, analytics rules and incidents, hunting with KQL, workbooks to visualize, playbooks (Logic Apps) to respond, UEBA and threat intelligence.
Sentinel is moving to the Defender portal; Azure portal support ends after March 31, 2027 (check the current date before an exam).

cheatSheet.heading: Defender XDR: match the product to the asset
points: Office 365 = email and collaboration (Safe Links, Safe Attachments; Plan 2 adds Threat Explorer, AIR and attack simulation). Endpoint = devices (ASR, EDR). Identity = on-premises AD (domain controller sensors). Cloud Apps = SaaS CASB (Cloud Discovery, session controls).
Vulnerability Management = find and prioritize weaknesses. Microsoft Threat Intelligence = threat analytics and intel. Advanced hunting = KQL over raw Defender data.
Defender portal (security.microsoft.com) unifies incidents, alerts, hunting and, increasingly, Sentinel; you only see licensed features.

cheatSheet.heading: Compliance: portals and trust
points: Service Trust Portal = Microsoft's audit reports, certifications and compliance guides. Purview portal = where you manage Purview solutions.
Six privacy principles: control, transparency, security, strong legal protections, no content-based targeting, benefits to you.
Compliance Manager = assessments, controls, improvement actions. Compliance score = progress on improvement actions, not proof of compliance.

cheatSheet.heading: Purview: information protection and lifecycle
points: Classify with sensitive information types, trainable classifiers and exact data match. Content explorer = what exists now. Activity explorer = what happened over time.
Sensitivity label = classify and protect (encrypt, mark) and travels with the content; it must be published with a label policy. DLP = detect and block risky sharing, including Endpoint DLP.
Retention policy = whole location, automatic. Retention label = individual item, can declare a record. Records management = locked content with disposition and proof of deletion.

cheatSheet.heading: Purview: insider risk, eDiscovery and audit
points: Insider risk management = risky activity by trusted people, with pseudonymized usernames. Communication compliance = monitor messages for violations.
eDiscovery = cases, legal holds, search, review, export. Premium adds custodians, review sets and analytics.

Audit (Standard) = on by default, 180 days. Audit (Premium) = retention policies, one year by default for Entra, Exchange, OneDrive and SharePoint (licensed users), up to 10 years with an add-on, and intelligent insights.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day reminders
points: Microsoft scores this 0 to 1000 with 700 to pass, not a flat percentage.
Watch for Defender for Cloud (infrastructure) versus Defender for Cloud Apps (SaaS CASB), and Entra roles versus Azure RBAC. They are the most common look-alike traps.
Read for the verb: "classify and protect" = sensitivity label, "stop sharing" = DLP, "keep or delete" = retention, "investigate a legal matter" = eDiscovery, "who did what" = Audit.

madlibs.scenario: A team moves a database from a server room to Azure virtual machines. Microsoft still protects the physical datacenter, but the team must patch the guest operating system and protect its accounts and data, because under the {b1} model the customer always keeps data, devices and {b2}. The company also wants every request verified regardless of network location, which is the {b3} model.
madlibs.explanation: Shared responsibility says data, devices and accounts and identities always stay with the customer. Zero Trust verifies explicitly, uses least privilege and assumes breach, and does not rely on network location.

madlibs.scenario: A user types a password and approves a prompt on a phone, which is {b1}. The system then checks which files the user may open, which is {b2}. Because the company's partner trusts that sign-in for its own apps, the arrangement is called {b3}.
madlibs.explanation: Authentication proves who you are, authorization decides what you can do, and federation is a trust between identity providers.

madlibs.scenario: A company wants to require MFA from outside the office. It builds a {b1} policy and tests it first in {b2} mode. Because it also wants sign-in risk to drive the decision, it needs {b3}.

options: Entra ID P2 with ID Protection

madlibs.explanation: Conditional Access evaluates signals and enforces controls such as MFA, and report-only mode shows the effect without enforcing. Risk-based conditions need ID Protection, a P2 feature.

madlibs.scenario: Administrators should hold the Security Administrator role only when needed, so the company uses {b1} to make them {b2} for the role and activate it with justification. Every quarter, managers confirm which guests still need access using {b3}.
madlibs.explanation: PIM provides eligible, just-in-time, time-limited privileged access, and access reviews periodically recertify who still needs access.

madlibs.scenario: A web shop is attacked with injected SQL in form fields, which a {b1} would block. Its public IPs are flooded with traffic, which {b2} mitigates. Administrators reach private VMs through {b3}, so the VMs need no public IP addresses.
madlibs.explanation: WAF defends web apps against exploits like SQL injection, DDoS Protection counters traffic floods, and Bastion provides RDP and SSH without exposing management ports or public IPs.

madlibs.scenario: A security team connects logs from many sources into {b1}, which acts as both a {b2} and a SOAR. When an alert fires, a {b3} automatically disables the compromised account.
madlibs.explanation: Sentinel is a SIEM and SOAR; playbooks (Azure Logic Apps) automate responses, while workbooks only visualize.

madlibs.scenario: A company labels contracts as Confidential using a {b1}, which only appears for staff after a {b2} publishes it. To stop confidential files being emailed outside, it adds a {b3} policy.
madlibs.explanation: Sensitivity labels classify and protect, label policies publish them to users, and DLP blocks risky sharing.

madlibs.scenario: The legal team needs to keep all mailboxes for seven years, which a {b1} does for the whole location. A single signed contract must be locked and cannot be deleted, so it is marked as a record with a {b2}. When a lawsuit starts, counsel uses {b3} to place a hold and collect content.
madlibs.explanation: Retention policies apply to locations, retention labels apply to items and can declare records, and eDiscovery provides holds and collection for legal cases.

sequences.prompt: Roll out a new Conditional Access policy safely. Put the steps in order.
steps: Exclude emergency access accounts from the policy
Create the policy with the report-only state
Review sign-in logs to see who would have been affected
Change the policy state to On to enforce it
sequences.explanation: Protect the break-glass accounts first, test in report-only mode, check the impact in the logs, and only then enforce so you do not lock people out.

sequences.prompt: Activate a privileged role with Privileged Identity Management. Put the steps in order.
steps: The user is made eligible for the role
The user requests activation and supplies MFA and a justification
An approver approves the request, if approval is required
The role is active for a limited time
The assignment expires automatically
sequences.explanation: Eligibility comes first, activation needs proof and sometimes approval, access is temporary, and it ends on its own.

sequences.prompt: A threat is detected and handled in Microsoft Sentinel. Put the steps in order.
steps: Data connectors ingest logs from the environment
An analytics rule detects suspicious activity and raises an alert
Related alerts are grouped into an incident
An automation rule triggers a playbook to respond
An analyst investigates and closes the incident
sequences.explanation: Data must be ingested before rules can detect anything, alerts roll up into incidents, and automation and analysts handle the response.

sequences.prompt: Protect documents with a sensitivity label. Put the steps in order.
steps: Create the sensitivity label with encryption and markings
Publish the label to users with a label policy
A user (or auto-labeling) applies the label to a document
The protection travels with the document when it is shared
sequences.explanation: A label must be created and then published before it can be applied; once applied, the protection stays with the content.

sequences.prompt: Run a legal investigation in Microsoft Purview eDiscovery. Put the steps in order.
steps: Create an eDiscovery case
Place legal holds on the relevant content sources
Search for the relevant content
Review the results
Export the content for counsel
sequences.explanation: Open the case, preserve the content with holds, search and review it, then export what counsel needs.

caseStudies.title: Adatum Health Secures Its Move to the Microsoft Cloud
caseStudies.scenario: Adatum Health keeps its staff accounts in on-premises Active Directory and wants everyone to use one identity for Microsoft 365 and for Azure. A web portal for patients runs in Azure and has been probed with SQL injection attempts, and its public addresses were once flooded with traffic. Administrators currently keep permanent high-level roles, and the compliance team wants them to receive these only when needed. Staff often email patient documents, and the privacy officer wants documents containing patient identifiers to be protected and prevented from leaving the company. Lawyers also need to preserve mailbox content when a claim is filed. Finally, the security operations team wants one place to collect logs from Azure, Microsoft 365 and a third-party firewall and to automate responses.

questions.question: Which approach gives staff one identity for Microsoft 365 and Azure while they keep their on-premises accounts?
options: Hybrid identity using Microsoft Entra Connect or Cloud Sync
Creating guest accounts for every employee
Placing every staff member in a network security group
questions.explanation: Hybrid identity synchronizes on-premises accounts with Entra ID so people keep a single identity. Guest accounts are for outsiders, and NSGs and Bastion are network features.

questions.question: Which pair of services best addresses the SQL injection attempts and the traffic flood against the patient portal?
options: Web Application Firewall and DDoS Protection
questions.explanation: WAF blocks web exploits such as SQL injection and DDoS Protection mitigates traffic floods. The other pairs address remote access and secrets, compliance, or email.

questions.question: Which Entra capability gives administrators high-level roles only when needed, with justification and a time limit?
questions.explanation: PIM provides just-in-time, time-bound activation of eligible roles with approval, justification and MFA options.

questions.question: Which two Purview solutions meet the privacy officer's and the lawyers' requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Sensitivity labels with data loss prevention
questions.explanation: Labels and DLP protect patient documents and stop them leaving, and eDiscovery with holds preserves mailbox content for claims. DDoS Protection and Vulnerability Management are not Purview solutions.

compare.scenario: A developer must store user passwords so that the system can verify them at login, but nobody, even with a stolen database, should be able to recover them. Which technique should be used?
compare.optionA: Encrypt each password with a shared symmetric key kept in the application settings.
compare.optionB: Store a salted hash of each password and compare hashes at login.
compare.why: Encryption is reversible by anyone who obtains the key, which is stored right next to the data here. A salted hash is one-way, so the original password cannot be recovered even if the database is stolen.

compare.scenario: A user has just proven who they are with a password and an app prompt. Which concept decides whether they may open the payroll folder?
compare.why: Authentication already finished when the user proved who they were. Deciding what that identity may open is authorization.

compare.scenario: A help desk technician must be able to reset passwords for users in the directory, and nothing else. Which permission system is the right place to grant this?
compare.optionA: A Microsoft Entra role scoped to the task, such as a password or helpdesk administrator.
compare.optionB: The Azure RBAC Contributor role on the subscription.
compare.why: Resetting directory passwords is a directory task, so an Entra role is needed. Azure RBAC governs Azure resources such as VMs and does not grant directory administration, and Contributor is far too broad anyway.

compare.scenario: An organization wants administrators to have no standing privileges and instead activate roles for two hours with a justification. Which feature matches?
compare.optionA: Access reviews that ask managers every quarter whether admins still need roles.
compare.optionB: Privileged Identity Management with eligible role assignments.
compare.why: Access reviews recertify access periodically but the admin still holds the role the rest of the time. PIM removes standing access and provides time-limited, just-in-time activation.

compare.scenario: A security team wants sign-in methods that cannot be captured by a fake login page. Which is better?
compare.optionA: A one-time code sent by SMS.
compare.optionB: A passkey stored on a FIDO2 security key.
compare.why: An SMS code can be typed into a phishing page and relayed. A passkey is bound to the real site, so it will not work on a lookalike page.

compare.scenario: A company wants a single managed service to control and log all outbound internet traffic from several virtual networks using FQDN rules and threat intelligence. Which fits better?
compare.optionB: A network security group on each subnet.
compare.why: NSGs are free layer 3 and 4 filters that are managed per subnet and cannot use FQDN rules or threat intelligence. Azure Firewall provides central control with those features.

compare.scenario: An application is being targeted with cross-site scripting in HTTP requests. Which control is the better fit?
compare.optionA: Azure Web Application Firewall on Application Gateway.
compare.why: DDoS Protection targets floods that exhaust capacity. Cross-site scripting hides in individual requests and needs a WAF that inspects layer 7.

compare.scenario: Management wants to discover which unsanctioned SaaS apps employees use and risk-score them. Which product fits?
compare.optionA: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps with Cloud Discovery.
compare.optionB: Microsoft Defender for Cloud with Defender CSPM.
compare.why: Defender for Cloud Apps is the CASB that discovers shadow IT. Defender for Cloud assesses posture of Azure and multicloud infrastructure, not employee use of SaaS apps.

compare.scenario: A SOC needs to ingest logs from Azure, Microsoft 365 and a third-party firewall, correlate them, and automate responses. Which is the better answer?
compare.why: Defender for Endpoint protects and monitors devices. Sentinel is a SIEM and SOAR that collects from many sources, including third-party ones, and automates response.

compare.scenario: The legal department wants every mailbox in the company kept for seven years without users having to do anything. Which is the simpler choice?
compare.optionA: A retention policy applied to Exchange locations.
compare.optionB: Retention labels that each user applies to individual emails.
compare.why: A policy applies automatically to all content in a location. Labels would depend on users tagging each item and would miss what they forget.

compare.scenario: An admin asks, "Which files in our SharePoint sites currently carry the Confidential label, and where are they?" Which tool answers this?
compare.why: Content explorer shows the current snapshot of labeled items and where they are. Activity explorer would show what happened to them, such as when labels were changed.

compare.scenario: Auditors require audit records for SharePoint and Exchange activity to be searchable for one year. Which edition is needed?
compare.optionA: Purview Audit (Standard), which is on by default.
compare.optionB: Purview Audit (Premium) with properly licensed users.
compare.why: Standard retains records for 180 days. Retention of one year by default for those services is a Premium capability, and it applies to users with the right license.
